Empirical Research Plan – “Going Public and Innovation”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
   • Core design: Two-stage least squares (2SLS) instrumental-variables difference-in-differences (IV-DiD).  
   • Source of quasi-random variation: unexpected NASDAQ return in the 60-day “quiet-period” after an S-1 filing.  
   • Logic: Within the universe of IPO filers (intent-to-treat population), the short-run market shock shifts the probability of completing the IPO but is orthogonal to the firm’s unobservable innovation trajectory. We exploit this shock to obtain the Local Average Treatment Effect (LATE) of becoming public on subsequent innovation outcomes.  
   • Estimand: β₂ in
        (Yit – Yit-1) = β₁ Postt + β₂ (Postt × IPOi) + λi + θt + εit  
     where IPOi is instrumented with NASDAQ₂m (quiet-period return). λi = firm FE; θt = calendar-year FE. The differencing or FE structure nets out firm-specific levels; Postt captures aggregate time effects; β₂ is the causal effect of actually going public relative to remaining private.

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  
   • Treatment variable: IPO_Completedi = 1 if firm i successfully lists within 12 months of its S-1 filing; 0 otherwise.  
   • Control group: Firms that filed an S-1 in the same calendar quarter but withdrew or allowed the filing to lapse. They represent the counterfactual of “would-be filers that stayed private.”  
   • Timing: Treatment starts on the IPO date (or withdrawal date for controls). Outcomes are measured yearly; the main window is three years pre- and five years post-event.

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  
   a) Relevance: Quiet-period NASDAQ return strongly predicts IPO completion. Plausibility: Numerous studies document elastic IPO supply to short-run market conditions. F-stat > 10 expected.  
   b) Exclusion (instrument exogeneity): Conditional on filing date, the NASDAQ shock affects the firm’s later innovation only through its effect on going public, not directly. Plausibility: individual firm cannot influence the broad index; shock occurs after disclosure freeze, before any post-IPO innovation could occur.  
   c) Monotonicity: A higher NASDAQ return weakly increases the likelihood of completion for every filer (no “defiers”). Reasonable given uniform underwriter incentives.  
   d) Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): One firm’s IPO status does not directly change another filer’s patents within the short horizon we analyze.  
   e) Parallel trends (for DiD component): Absent IPO completion, innovation time paths of successful and withdrawn filers would evolve similarly.

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS  
   1. Direct macro-innovation shocks: A NASDAQ surge may signal broader tech optimism that also raises all firms’ patenting.  
      • Mitigation: Include industry-by-year fixed effects; include contemporaneous NASDAQ return directly in the second stage; conduct placebo tests on pre-filing years.  
   2. Selection on filing timing: Savvy managers might time filings just before expected market runs.  
      • Mitigation: Use only the unexpected component of NASDAQ returns (residual from AR(1) forecast) as the instrument; show balance tests on filer observables across the NASDAQ return distribution.  
   3. Post-IPO capital infusion channel vs. disclosure/proprietary-cost channel: Multiple mechanisms could drive innovation change.  
      • Mitigation: Explore heterogeneous effects by ex-ante cash need, VC backing, and underwriter capacity; instrument captures the net total effect, but mechanism tests help interpretation.

5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
# ---- 0. Packages ----
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(fixest); library(ivreg); library(lmtest); library(sandwich)

# ---- 1. Load Data ----
ipo   <- read_csv("ipo_filings_1985_2003.csv")         # S-1 filers, completion flag, dates
pat   <- read_csv("firm_year_patents.csv")             # patent counts & quality by firm-year
nasdq <- read_csv("nasdaq_quietperiod_returns.csv")    # 60-day return after filing

# ---- 2. Merge & Construct Variables ----
df <- ipo %>%
  left_join(nasdq, by = "firm_id") %>%
  left_join(pat , by = c("firm_id","year")) %>%
  mutate(
    post       = ifelse(year >= event_year, 1, 0),      # event_year = IPO date or withdrawal date
    ipo_status = ifelse(completed == 1, 1, 0),
    patent_ln  = log(1 + patent_count),
    citations  = fwd_cites_per_patent,
    originality= patent_originality,
    instrument = nasdaq_ret_60d
  )

# Keep ±5-year window around event
df <- df %>% filter(year %in% (event_year-3):(event_year+5))

# ---- 3. Baseline 2SLS FE model ----
# Example outcome: log patent count
iv_formula <- patent_ln ~ post*ipo_status | post*instrument
model1 <- feols(iv_formula,
                data = df,
                fe = ~ firm_id + year)

# Cluster by firm
model1 <- coeftest(model1, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~ firm_id)
print(model1)

# ---- 4. Robustness: Pre-trend placebo (lead years as outcome) ----
df_placebo <- df %>% filter(year <= event_year - 1)
iv_placebo <- patent_ln ~ lead(post,1)*ipo_status | lead(post,1)*instrument
placebo <- feols(iv_placebo, data = df_placebo, fe = ~ firm_id + year)
coeftest(placebo, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~ firm_id)

# ---- 5. Robustness: Alternative outcome (citations per patent) ----
iv_formula2 <- citations ~ post*ipo_status | post*instrument
model2 <- feols(iv_formula2, data = df, fe = ~ firm_id + year)
coeftest(model2, vcov = vcovCL, cluster = ~ firm_id)
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  
   Theory is ambiguous. Going public supplies capital (+ patents) but heightens disclosure and short-term pressure (– long-run, risky research). Prior empirical work suggests:  
   • Quantity rises modestly (≈ 10–15 % more patents).  
   • Quality (citations/originality) declines (≈ 10 % lower).  
   Hence, expect β₂ > 0 for patent counts, β₂ < 0 for forward citations per patent and originality.

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST (1 = good, 0 = concern)  
   • First-stage relevance ................. 1  
   • Exclusion restriction / no direct path  0.8  
   • Parallel trends (pre-trend evidence) .. 0.8  
   • No selective filing around shocks ..... 0.7  
   • Correct outcome measurement ........... 0.9  
   Overall: 4.2 / 5 – credible but must document robustness thoroughly.
